newsitem.title: DUBAI: UAE interested in F-16, Rafale for $6 billion deal.
newsitem.headline: UAE interested in F-16, Rafale for $6 billion deal.

text.p: The United Arab Emirates has officially told the United States of its interest in the F-16 Block 60 warplane in a deal possibly worth $6 billion, dropping the rival U.S. F-15 but keeping the French Rafale in the contest, official military sources said on Wednesday.

A senior UAE official told Reuters McDonnell Douglas Corp's F-15 was taken out of the contest for up to 80 warplanes, with Lockheed Martin Corp, also of the United States, and France's Dassault Aviation the remaining bidders.
"From the American offers we have picked the F-16 over the F-15," he added.

The UAE "is still interested in a small added number of (French) Mirage 2000s and also looking at the Rafale as a competitor to the F-16", said the official who is close to the negotiations for the deal which could be the last of its size this century.

The UAE, which has several large arms deals with France, already has 36 Mirage 2000s, made by Dassault, in service and is looking to complement the fleet but the bulk of the deal is being contested by the F-16 and Dassault's Rafale.

Officials said the Gulf Arab state would not request further in-country trials by competing aircraft, adding that the selection process in the long-awaited, fiercely-contested deal could take another "few months".
Industry sources said both the F-16, with UAE specification, and the latest French land and sea-borne Rafale could be available for export by the year 2000 or slightly beyond.
Original bidders included Britain with an offer to lease Tornado aircraft while Abu Dhabi awaits the development of the Eurofighter 2000 but the UAE eliminated it at an earlier stage.
McDonnell Douglas, which has a deal with Saudi Arabia for 72 F-15S aircraft worth more than $9 billion, had offered the UAE the F-15.
The UAE, steadily becoming a key player on the international arms market, has a requirement for multi-role, long-range aircraft with superior air-to-air combat capability.

Lockheed had offered the F-16 Block 60 along with a Delta wing F-16U that would have been developed especially to meet the UAE's requirement but Abu Dhabi earlier dropped the latter as co-development costs were estimated at more than $2 billion.
Industry experts say the UAE's latest decision would further heat up the competition between the Rafale and the F-16 and could result in new bids by both makers to sweeten the deal.
"Now the U.S. can concentrate its rallying efforts to one American company, while the French will intensify efforts to secure the deal," one said.

Senior French, British and U.S. officials have in recent months been in contact with Abu Dhabi to help secure the deal for their arms makers, save jobs at home and give their aerospace industries a much-needed boost in a shrinking market.
Makers are also placing much hope on the deal to secure funds to finance next-generation warplanes at a time of weak demand at home with the end of the Cold War.
